title: Semantic shingling & tenant namespace review - Pinecrest Labs
summary: Deep technical review of semantic shingling (prompt windows), cache key namespaces, and multi-tenant safety for Pinecrest's on-prem inference pilot. Discussed hit-rate expectations, salted key strategies, eviction policies, VPC constraints, and fallback model routing. Agreed to run a 48h mixed-workload simulation and a focused 1M-request prefix collision test.
topics: semantic shingling vs simple prefix caching
batching windows and latency SLO impact
fallback routing to smaller model variants
transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date: 2026-06-17
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Ava Martin (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Pinecrest Head ML), Marco Ruiz (Pinecrest Infra), Priya Singh (Pinecrest CTO)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, we'll run through the semantic shingling approach and how we recommend namespacing keys for multi-tenant on-prem setups. Quick note, Samir is going to do the deep parts, i'll jump in on product/ops points.
[00:14] Dr. Lena: Great, we mainly want to understand collision risk and whether shingling affects latency in your runtime, also our security folks want to make sure no cross-tenant leakage.
[00:28] Samir: Totally. So first, semantic shingling is where we store overlapping n-gram prompt windows as cache entries rather than single fixed prefixes. It increases hit rate for conversational flows that mutate the tail, but it also increases the key cardinality if you don't compress the signatures.
[00:45] Marco: When you say "compress the signatures" do you mean hashing? We're on-prem with a KMS; we can't send raw prompts offsite.
[00:57] Samir: Yes hashing + HMAC with a per-tenant salt. Practically we compute: HMAC_SHA256(salt || normalize(prompt_shingle)) and store that as the cache key. The salt is tenant-specific and kept in your KMS/HSM. That avoids cross-tenant collisions even if prompt texts coincide.
[01:15] Priya: Our security lead asked about salt rotation — does that invalidate the cache?
[01:22] Ava: Good question. Salt rotation will invalidate entries unless you plan a migration window. We usually recommend key-versioned salts with a short overlap period: two-version acceptor where the server accepts both current and previous salt for reads during rotation. That keeps hit rates while rotating.
[01:38] Dr. Lena: And the hit rate numbers — do you have empirical from similar customers?
[01:44] Samir: Yes — for mixed conversational workloads we see shingling move hit rates from ~12-18% with prefix-only to ~30-45% depending on shingle size and user behavior. But that's workload dependent. If you have lots of paraphrase, shingling with semantic hashing (embedding-based buckets) helps.
[02:02] Marco: Wait embeddings for keys? our nodes are quantized, will that blow up compute?
[02:10] Samir: Embedding-based locality sensitive hashing (LSH) is an optional layer: you compute an embed for the prompt and bucket typical paraphrases. The cost is one embed call per candidate cache insertion/lookup — we can piggyback on your existing embedding pipeline or do a light-weight int8 quantized embed model on the same node. Latency add is usually 5-12 ms if done well, but it's configuration dependent.
[02:26] Dr. Lena: Sounds reasonable. On the runtime side, how does this interact with KV cache in the Redwood engine?
[02:33] Samir: Two places: 1) Prefix/prompt cache is a higher-level cache in front of the model runtime—if you hit it we return tokens without touching GPU. 2) KV cache is the model's internal attention key-value cache used to speed generation across tokens. Shingling reduces calls that reach the runtime, so it indirectly reduces KV cache churn. We also have a hotset eviction policy to keep frequently-reused KV pages resident.
[02:53] Marco: In on-prem mode with limited GPU memory, eviction is a big deal. What's your recommendation for hotset size vs tenant isolation?
[03:01] Samir: Isolate by tenant groups only in the cache namespace, but we avoid hard physical partitioning of GPU memory unless you're on dedicated capacity. For on-prem with mixed tenants, we recommend soft quotas per tenant and an LRU with weighted recency: weight by token-cost of entry. That prevents small tenants from thrashing hot KV pages.
[03:22] Priya: If a tenant is noisy, can we quarantine them?
[03:26] Ava: Yes — Redwood has tenant quarantine rules: rate-limits, circuit breakers, and automatic fallback to a smaller quantized model variant when noise crosses thresholds. It's a graceful degradation path.
[03:36] Dr. Lena: About quantization — we plan to use 4-bit quant for cost. Does quantization affect cacheability of outputs? We've seen artifacts where answers differ slightly and then downstream systems treat them as different.
[03:48] Samir: Quantization can change token output probabilities hence final tokens; for deterministic caches we normalize outputs before storing only if you accept a bit of post-processing. Another approach is to store model-agnostic semantic keys (embeddings of the canonical response) and allow fuzzy-hit matching. That trades precision for higher hit-rate.
[04:05] Marco: Fuzzy hits — risk of returning semantically similar but factually stale responses?
[04:11] Samir: Correct. We mitigate that by adding TTLs and versioning metadata: each cache entry stores model_version, quant_profile, and creation timestamp. If your eval suite sees regressions, Redwood Optimize can flag and auto-invalidate by model_version.
[04:29] [00:05:00]
Samir: Latency notes — shingling increases key-lookup time slightly because of multiple candidate lookups per request. But we reduce backend GPU calls more often, saving net latency. For tight SLOs (p95 < 150ms) we usually recommend a single-shot shallow shingle lookup plus a single async-prefetch for larger matches. If that async-prefetch wins, we patch the response via a second chunked stream (we support streaming patching).
[05:05] Dr. Lena: Our SLO is 120ms p95 for front-end requests; can you guarantee that with shingling?
[05:12] Samir: Guarantees require measurement on your infra, but we've seen configurations that meet 120ms p95 using a 10-20ms local key lookup + immediate return on cache hit. For misses, model fallthrough adds GPU latency. We can route critical routes to dedicated capacity to lock latencies.
[05:30] Marco: On VPC/on-prem networking — we're air-gapped during evaluation. Can Redwood run wholly in our VPC with a private control plane?
[05:39] Ava: Yes, Redwood Private can run with a private control plane and optional on-prem package. For air-gapped setups, we ship the runtime and local management agent; audit logs are stored locally and optional push to your SIEM. The only challenge is initial model onboarding and optional telemetry — both can be done via secure transfer.
[05:56] Priya: For keys we need HSM integration; do you support AWS CloudHSM and on-prem YubiHSM?
[06:02] Samir: We support major KMSs and HSMs; on-prem HSMs integrated via PKCS#11 or a secrets proxy. We recommend keeping salt and any tenant key material in your HSM and never exposing them to the Redwood control plane.
[06:13] [00:21:00]
Dr. Lena: Let's talk experiments — what should we measure to validate the shingling approach?
[06:20] Samir: Minimum: 1) end-to-end p95 latency with and without shingling, 2) cache hit-rate by route, 3) false positive fuzzy hits (if used), 4) collision rate for salted keys, 5) KV eviction frequency and GPU memory pressure, 6) tail latencies during a noisy tenant spike.
[06:40] Marco: For collision testing — how do you simulate?
[06:44] Samir: We can run a synthetic test with a controlled corpus — generate 1M prompt shingle candidates across 500 tenants and measure HMAC collisions and effective cardinality. We'll use your tokenization rules and normalization pipeline to be faithful.
[06:58] Priya: Do you have tooling to replay production-ish traffic without sending PII?
[07:03] Ava: Yes — Redwood provides a replay harness that can anonymize logs and replay approximate load distributions. We usually recommend a two-phase test: a small staged run on your infra and a larger 48h run to capture diurnal patterns.
[07:20] [00:38:00]
Samir: Quick note on key normalization — normalize whitespace, unicode NFKC, and canonicalize trailing punctuation for consistent keys. Also strip session-specific ephemeral tokens before shingling.
[07:33] Dr. Lena: Our production prompts include session IDs occasionally buried in user text, how do you strip that?
[07:38] Samir: We provide a customizable scrubber — regex rules live in your config. For stricter compliance we recommend doing scrubbing before hashing inside your trusted environment.
[07:48] Marco: Anything about RBAC? our infra team wants to ensure only certain roles can change salt configs.
[07:54] Ava: Redwood Console supports RBAC and audit trails for salt rotation, model_version promotion, and cache invalidation. Those actions can be tied to SSO/SAML groups.
[08:04] Priya: Let's quickly talk rollout strategy — we don't want to flip shingling on globally.
[08:09] Samir: Start with a single low-risk route, run sample-based shingling in shadow mode to collect metrics without changing responses. Then a canary with 5-10% traffic and strict rollback if hit-rate regressions or latency problems appear. Also run A/B on a subset of tenants.
[08:28] Dr. Lena: What's the expected ops overhead? Marco will want concrete numbers.
[08:31] Marco: yes please.
[08:33] Samir: Initial engineering time: ~2-4 engineer-weeks for integration (includes KMS integration, scrubber tuning, and the replay harness). For ongoing ops: expect 0.1-0.3 FTE once tuned; most day-to-day is alerting on hit-rate regressions.
[08:48] Ava: Ok, to wrap up we'll share a benchmark plan and a configurator spreadsheet.
[08:52] Priya: Good. If we see acceptable hit rates and no leakage, we'll move to a 6-week pilot on a single compute cluster.
[08:59] [00:59:00]
Ava: Thanks everyone. We'll capture next steps.

End of transcript
